financial_advisory_ria.structure_note: This industry has a structural feature unlike anything else built in this dataset so far: a FEDERAL/STATE JURISDICTIONAL SPLIT based on assets under management (AUM), not a single state regulator. CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 directly against the Texas State Securities Board's (TSSB) own FAQ: an adviser with AUM under $100 million generally registers with TSSB under the Texas Securities Act; an adviser whose AUM grows to $100 million or more must apply for SEC registration within 90 days of filing an annual Form ADV amendment reporting that threshold (SEC Rule 203A-1, 17 CFR Section 275.203A-1). A genuinely easy-to-miss nuance: SEC registration does NOT eliminate all Texas-level obligations -- an SEC-registered adviser with Texas clients must still make a Texas NOTICE FILING and pay applicable fees. Private fund advisers with less than $25 million AUM can instead file as Exempt Reporting Advisers (ERA) in Texas without full registration. Filings run through the IARD (Investment Adviser Registration Depository) system for the firm-level Form ADV, and the CRD system for individual Investment Adviser Representative (IAR) Form U4 filings -- FINRA operates this technical infrastructure but has no regulatory authority over investment advisers itself; TSSB or the SEC is the actual regulator depending on which jurisdiction applies. This file has NOT independently pinned an exact Texas-specific books-and-records rule citation (TSSB generally follows a 'substantially similar' standard to the federal Rule 204-2, per NASAA's Model Rule 203(a)-2, but the precise Texas Administrative Code section was not confirmed in this research pass) -- verify against current TSSB rules before treating a specific Texas citation as confirmed the way the federal Rule 204-2 citation is.

Form ADV (Parts 1 & 2) -- TSSB or SEC Fi: Jurisdictional split CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 directly against TSSB's own FAQ: advisers with AUM under $100 million generally register with TSSB (Texas Securities Act); advisers with AUM of $100 million or more must apply for SEC registration within 90 days of filing an annual Form ADV amendment reporting that threshold (SEC Rule 203A-1, 17 CFR Section 275.203A-1). Private fund advisers under $25 million AUM may instead file as an Exempt Reporting Adviser (ERA) in Texas.
Texas Notice Filing (if SEC-registered w: CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 directly against TSSB's own FAQ: an investment adviser already registered with, or seeking registration with, the SEC must still make a notice filing in Texas and pay applicable fees if it has Texas clients -- SEC registration does not eliminate this state-level obligation.
Investment Adviser Representative Regist: Individual Investment Adviser Representatives (IARs) register via Form U4, filed electronically through the CRD system -- a separate system from IARD, which handles the firm-level Form ADV.
Books and Records Retention Log: For SEC-registered advisers: SEC Rule 204-2 (17 CFR Section 275.204-2) under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Most records must be retained for at least 5 years from the end of the fiscal year in which the record was created, with the most recent 2 years immediately accessible at the firm's principal office. Corporate/organizational records (partnership agreements, charters, minute books) must be retained for the life of the entity plus 3 years after dissolution. CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 across multiple independent sources. For state-registered (TSSB) advisers, requirements are generally 'substantially similar' per NASAA's Model Rule 203(a)-2, but this file has NOT independently confirmed the precise Texas Administrative Code citation -- verify before relying on a specific Texas-only figure.
Annual Compliance Review Records: SEC Rule 206(4)-7 (the 'Compliance Rule') under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 -- requires SEC-registered advisers to adopt and implement written policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations, and to review those policies and procedures at least annually.
Custody Rule Compliance Records (if appl: Applies only when the adviser has custody of client funds or securities (e.g. direct fee deduction with certain safeguards, or actual possession of client assets) -- triggers additional safeguarding, surprise-examination, and qualified-custodian requirements under the SEC's Custody Rule (17 CFR Section 275.206(4)-2). Not every adviser has custody; verify the specific tenant's actual practices before assuming this category applies.
